evidence_quote: the analyses exploit the random assignment that results from lottery-based admissions for a small set of schools
resolved_title: Can Interdistrict Choice Boost Student Achievement? The Case of Connecticut's Interdistrict Magnet School Program
notes: Lottery sample of applicants to interdistrict magnet schools (central-city students who applied), so universal with opt_in = 1 per codebook. Kraft n 514 to 516 matches the WWC full-sample lottery analysis; the abstract does not state the grade, WWC lists grade 8 (magnet middle schools). Abstract only.

evidence_quote: A pretest-posttest cluster-randomized trial involving 31 middle schools and 335 students with disabilities tested the effects of combining explicit and anchored instruction on fraction computation and problem solving.
resolved_title: Effects of Blended Instructional Models on Math Performance
notes: Sample is students with disabilities taught in special education resource rooms (WWC: all were identified as having disabilities in mathematics). Tie-breaker 4: special-education sample is targeted_other even though the students are described as low performing in math. Abstract gives 335 students, Kraft n_max 323 is the analytic sample. WWC pct_iep 0.00 looks like a data entry error given the sample.

evidence_quote: This study uses data from a 5-year longitudinal randomized controlled effectiveness trial of SWPBIS conducted in 37 elementary schools
resolved_title: Examining the Effects of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Student Outcomes
notes: Schoolwide universal program randomized across 37 Maryland elementary schools in five rural and suburban districts (WWC setting); no student or school eligibility rule stated in the abstract or WWC text. Kraft n 11738 matches the WWC full sample. Abstract only.

evidence_quote: We examined the effects of the Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) for opinion essay writing among 380 eighth grade students in six urban middle schools in a major city in Portugal.
resolved_title: Professional development in Self-Regulated Strategy Development: Effects on the writing performance of eighth grade Portuguese students
notes: Codebook worked example. Schools matched in pairs on SES and randomized; no student rule stated. International setting (Portugal). Outcome is writing quality, not a broad reading test. Abstract only.

evidence_quote: At-risk students (n = 259) were randomly assigned to intervention and control.
resolved_title: Improving at-risk learners' understanding of fractions
notes: Codebook worked example. WWC setting text confirms the rule: participants scored below the 35th percentile on a whole-number calculation screener. Twin of 323-fuchs-2013 (same article entered twice by Kraft with different effect lists); identical codes. Abstract only.

evidence_quote: At-risk students (n = 259) were randomly assigned to intervention and control.
resolved_title: Improving at-risk learners' understanding of fractions
notes: Codebook worked example. WWC setting text confirms the rule: participants scored below the 35th percentile on a whole-number calculation screener. Twin of 322-fuchs-2013 (same article entered twice by Kraft with different effect lists); identical codes. Abstract only.

evidence_quote: In this randomized controlled trial involving 312 students enrolled in an after-school program, the authors generated intention-to-treat and treatment-on-the-treated estimates of the program’s impact on several literacy outcomes of fourth, fifth, and sixth graders reading below proficiency on a state assessment at baseline.
resolved_title: Can a Mixed-Method Literacy Intervention Improve the Reading Achievement of Low-Performing Elementary School Students in an After-School Program? Results From a Randomized Controlled Trial of READ 180 Enterprise (Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 2011)
notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: the abstract (DOI 10.3102/0162373711399148) is Kim, Capotosto, Hartry, and Fitzgerald 2011, the peer-reviewed version of the Brockton READ 180 after-school trial that Kraft cites as the Fitzgerald and Hartry 2008 phase II report, which is not online; same trial and same eligibility rule. Students were fourth to sixth graders reading below proficiency on the state test who enrolled in the after-school program, so targeted_low with opt_in 1. The wwc-codes.csv row for 284 adds that Brockton chose four of its 16 schools for having many students reading below grade level, so level is both. Kraft's n 293 to 296 are the 2008 report's cohort figures; the abstract's 312 is the journal sample. Kraft rows 491-kim-2011 and 494-kim-2010 describe the same trial. Abstract-only, so medium.

evidence_quote: In this randomized controlled trial involving 312 students enrolled in an after-school program, the authors generated intention-to-treat and treatment-on-the-treated estimates of the program's impact on several literacy outcomes of fourth, fifth, and sixth graders reading below proficiency on a state assessment at baseline.
resolved_title: Can a mixed-method literacy intervention improve the reading achievement of low-performing elementary school students in an after-school program? Results from a randomized controlled trial of READ 180 Enterprise
notes: Students enrolled in an after-school program (opt_in) and were reading below proficiency on the MCAS at baseline; the WWC text says 95 percent, not all, scored below proficiency, so the rule was not a strict cutoff. This is the Cohort 1 first-year sample (297 students per WWC) of the Brockton READ 180 trial also reported in 284-fitzgerald-2008 and 494-kim-2010. Kraft n 296 matches the WWC full sample. Abstract only.

evidence_quote: administered during an hour-long after-school program to groups of randomly selected students in grades 4-6 who were identified as struggling readers prior to randomization
resolved_title: A randomized experiment of a mixed-methods literacy intervention for struggling readers in grades 4-6: Effects on word reading efficiency, reading comprehension and vocabulary, and oral reading fluency
notes: The abstract (ERIC) states only that 294 children in grades 4 to 6 were randomly assigned to READ 180 or a district after-school program; the title and the WWC setting text both say the students were struggling readers identified before randomization, so the two sources agree and confidence is medium rather than low. After-school program implies enrollment (opt_in). Second-year combined-cohort sample of the Brockton READ 180 trial (see 284-fitzgerald-2008, 491-kim-2011). Kraft n 264 matches the WWC full analytic sample.

evidence_quote: Students who were identified as English language learners (ELLs) and were eligible for mainstreaming were randomly assigned to classrooms participating in the study.
resolved_title: WWC Review of the Report: A Randomized Experiment of a Cognitive Strategies Approach to Text-Based Analytical Writing for Mainstreamed Latino English Language Learners in Grades 6 to 12
notes: DATA NOTE: text/493-kim-2011.txt is the WWC single study review (August 2012) of the Kim, Olson et al. 2011 JREE article, not the article itself, so confidence is medium. All 2,726 students were English learners eligible for mainstreaming in Santa Ana USD; selection on ELL status, not on a score. Kraft n 1393 to 2721 matches the WWC analysis samples. The codebook worked example 483-kim-2011 (another batch) is the same Pathway Project study, so rows 483 and 493 look like a cross-batch twin; codes should match.

evidence_quote: SRI's research design for the evaluation was to randomly assign 44 rural high-poverty school districts to either the CRWP program or a control group.
resolved_title: Impact of the National Writing Project's College-Ready Writers Program on Teachers and Students (SRI research brief, November 2015)
notes: Codebook worked example. Districts selected on rurality and poverty; no student rule; all grade 7 to 10 English classes took part. Twin of 339-gallagher-2017 (another batch); identical codes. The source is the 5-page SRI research brief. Outcome is argument writing on the Analytic Writing Continuum, not a broad reading test. Kraft n 2486 matches the WWC full sample.

evidence_quote: This paper reports on a randomized experiment to study the impact of an alternative teacher preparation program, Teach for America (TFA), on student achievement and other outcomes.
resolved_title: Alternative routes to teaching: The impacts of Teach for America on student achievement and other outcomes
notes: Neither the abstract nor the WWC text states how the 17 schools in six TFA regions were chosen; the WWC only reports demographics (95 percent FRL). The design (schools where TFA placed teachers) suggests targeted_other at the school level through TFA's own placement rule, but no source available here says so, so unclear per the codebook. Students were randomly assigned to TFA or non-TFA teachers within schools, grades 1 to 5. Kraft n 1715 matches the WWC sample. Abstract only.

evidence_quote: The current study examines whether Word Generation (WG), a Tier-I discussion-based program designed to build academic literacy and linguistic practices, provides differential gains for non-ELL and ELL students
resolved_title: Reducing academic inequalities for English language learners: Variation in experimental effects of Word Generation in high-poverty schools
notes: DATA PROBLEM: the WWC row (85771) is Kim, Hemphill, Troyer et al. 2017 on STARI (grades 6 to 8, about 400 students), not the Kim, Hsin, and Snow 2018 Word Generation paper Kraft cites (n 2160 to 2226, grades 4 to 7); the WWC match is wrong and its sample text was not used. The abstract describes a universal Tier-I program in high-poverty schools but never states how schools or students were selected, so unclear. Kraft's two effects (0.03, 0.03) may be full-sample reading comprehension estimates by year or ELL versus non-ELL subgroup estimates; cannot tell from the abstract. Abstract only.

evidence_quote: The lowest-ranking schools were designated as potential receiving schools that could benefit from the intervention, and the rest were potential sending schools.
resolved_title: Transfer Incentives for High-Performing Teachers: Final Results from a Multisite Randomized Experiment (Executive Summary, NCEE 2014-4004)
notes: Text file is the executive summary only. Study schools were the receiving schools, chosen as the lowest-ranked schools in each district by students' average prior achievement (21 percent of schools); teacher teams with vacancies in those schools were randomized. Districts were chosen for size and economic diversity. No student-level rule; all students of the teacher teams were analyzed. Kraft n 6103 (reading, grades 3 to 8) is plausible for the pooled team-level sample.

evidence_quote: program participation was made available to every K-8 classroom teacher, as well as reading and math interventionists. Approximately 160 teachers were eligible to participate in the experiment.
resolved_title: Enhancing the Efficacy of Teacher Incentives through Loss Aversion: A Field Experiment (NBER Working Paper 18237)
notes: Nine schools in Chicago Heights, IL; every K-8 teacher was eligible and 150 of 160 opted in, then teachers were randomized to incentive arms. Students were all students of participating teachers; the district is 98 percent FRL but nothing in the design selected on poverty or achievement. Teacher opt-in, not student opt-in, so opt_in = 0. Kraft n 900 to 1016 is well below the roughly 150 classrooms in the trial; Kraft's rows may be a grade-band or test subsample (ISAT grades 3 to 8 versus ITBS K to 2). Kraft cites the 2012 working paper.

evidence_quote: The 32 school leaders who volunteered to join the experimental sample represented a diverse array of elementary schools in terms of prior achievement, demographics, and geography.
resolved_title: The Impact of Achieve3000 on Elementary Literacy Outcomes: Randomized Control Trial Evidence, 2013-14 to 2014-15 (WCPSS DRA Report No. 16.02)
notes: Wake County elementary schools were eligible after removing the 12 pilot schools and SuccessMaker schools; 32 volunteering schools were paired on 2013 reading composites and randomized (16 treatment, 16 control); all students in grades 2 to 5 in those schools were in the sample. Volunteering is not selection on need (tie-breaker 6). Kraft n 6235 to 12851 fits the annual and pooled analytic samples. Not in the WWC export; manual match accepted WWC study 85405, the same DRA report.

evidence_quote: All participating schools met the following criteria for inclusion in the project: (a) is an elementary school; (b) has been implementing positive behavioral interventions and supports (PBIS) for at least 1 year, as documented by district records
resolved_title: A Randomized Waitlist Controlled Analysis of Team-Initiated Problem Solving Professional Development and Use
notes: Thirty-eight K-5 schools in North Carolina and Oregon, recruited as a convenience sample of schools already implementing PBIS and using SWIS with a monthly team meeting; criteria are implementation features, not need or achievement (tie-breaker 6). All students in the schools are the student sample. Kraft n 2765 to 2984 is far below the WWC full sample of 18,443 students, so Kraft's math effects may come from a grade-level subsample or a companion report; the journal article itself reports team-process outcomes, and the student achievement results are not described in this text.

evidence_quote: to be eligible for Higher Achievement, students and their parents needed to complete an application, attend an in-person interview and commit to active participation for three to four years.
resolved_title: Staying On Track: Testing Higher Achievement's Long-Term Impact on Academic Outcomes and High School Choice
notes: Lottery among 952 applicants (rising 5th and 6th graders) to five Higher Achievement centers in DC and Alexandria, so universal with opt_in = 1 per the codebook. No achievement or income rule at the student level; applicants scored slightly above the national average and 60 percent were FRL. Caveat: the program sites its centers in 'at-risk communities' and recruits mainly through school referrals, which a reviewer could read as targeted_other at the site level; coded on the applicant lottery rule and confidence set to medium for that reason. Kraft n 719 to 815 fits the follow-up analytic samples.

evidence_quote: they selected districts to participate if they were in an urbanized area of Alaska, agreed to participate in the study, and anticipated new teacher hires.
resolved_title: Mentoring Early Career Teachers in Urban Alaska: Impact Findings from the Investing in Innovation (i3) Evaluation of the Alaska Statewide Mentor Project Urban Growth Opportunity
notes: Teacher-level randomization of first-year teachers in five urban Alaska districts; the student sample is all students of the randomized early career teachers in tested grades (grades 4 to 6 self-contained classrooms and secondary math and language arts). Districts chosen for urbanicity and hiring, not need. Kraft n 263 to 2631 fits the student analytic samples by grade band and subject. Long i3 report; read the evaluation design and sample sections only.

evidence_quote: A 2-step process was used to establish student eligibility for System 44. The Scholastic Reading Inventory (SRI) was used to screen students in Grades 4-8 who performed below the 50th percentile on the spring 2010 California Standards Test (CST) for System 44 eligibility.
resolved_title: Evaluation of System 44: Final Report (RMC Research, November 2011)
notes: Students in grades 4 to 8 below the 50th percentile on the CST were screened with the SRI (below 600 Lexiles) and then the Scholastic Phonics Inventory; those in the Beginning or Developing reader categories (425 students) were randomized. One large suburban southern California district, 2010-11. Kraft n 287 to 340 matches the analytic samples. Manual WWC match: accepted 89969 (this 2011 report); 66-beam-2012 is a separate 2011-12 trial of the same program, not a twin.

evidence_quote: Students who performed below the 50th percentile on the fall 2011 MEAP or below the 25th percentile on the spring 2011 AIMSweb assessment were subsequently tested for System 44 eligibility.
resolved_title: Evaluation of System 44: Final Report (RMC Research, September 2012)
notes: Urban Michigan district, 2011-12, 16 schools, grades 4 to 8. Target sample chosen on MEAP or AIMSweb performance, then screened with SRI (below 600 Lexiles) and the Scholastic Phonics Inventory; 368 eligible students randomized, 317 received the allocated condition, which matches Kraft n_max 317. The evaluators purposefully oversampled students with learning disabilities, but the rule is achievement-based, so targeted_low (tie-breaker 1). Manual WWC match: accepted 89968 (this 2012 report). Separate trial from 65-beam-2011 (different district and year), not a twin.

evidence_quote: To qualify for the study, schools had to meet requirements under Title I (schoolwide or targeted) or Missouri's historical requirements for Title II.D (50 percent of students in poverty) and be part of the Small Rural School Achievement program or the Rural and Low-Income School program
resolved_title: The Impact of eMINTS Professional Development on Teacher Instruction and Student Achievement: Year 1 Report
notes: High-poverty rural Missouri middle schools selected on Title I or 50 percent poverty plus rural program membership; schools randomized; all grade 7 and 8 students in study schools. Kraft n 3430 matches the WWC Year 1 report sample. The WWC row cites the 2016 EEPA article by Meyers, Molefe, Brandt, Zhu, and Dhillon on the same trial; Kraft cites the Year 1 report.

evidence_quote: We focused recruitment efforts on districts with large concentrations of secondary math teachers from TFA or a Teaching Fellows program.
resolved_title: The Effectiveness of Secondary Math Teachers from Teach For America and the Teaching Fellows Programs (NCEE 2013-4015)
notes: Study schools were those with eligible classroom matches containing a TFA or Teaching Fellows math teacher; both programs place teachers only in high-need schools (report p. xxiii: 82 percent of TFA study schools Title I eligible). Coded targeted_other at the school level on the program's own placement rule, as with the codebook's AmeriCorps example; a reviewer could argue universal because the evaluators themselves imposed no need criterion, hence medium confidence. Students were randomly assigned to classes within schools; no student rule. Kraft n 710 to 4573 matches the WWC grade-band samples (grades 6 to 8: 3,373; grades 6 to 12: 4,573). Long report; read the executive summary and Chapter II recruitment section only.

evidence_quote: We focused our recruitment efforts on districts and other TFA placement partners with large concentrations of elementary teachers from TFA.
resolved_title: Impacts of the Teach For America Investing in Innovation Scale-Up (Mathematica final report, March 4, 2015)
notes: Same design logic as 170-clark-2013: schools entered the sample because they employed first- or second-year TFA corps members, and TFA places corps members in low-income schools (report p. 8: 84 percent of 2012-13 corps members in schools with 60 percent or more FRL; study schools 97 percent Title I). Coded targeted_other at the school level on the program placement rule, medium confidence for the same reason. Students randomized to TFA or comparison teachers within schools, grades PK to 5. Kraft n 313 to 2123 matches the WWC subsamples (grades 3 to 5: 412 to 470; full: 2,065 to 2,123). Only test-score data for students whose parents consented, which is a consent condition rather than program opt-in.

evidence_quote: We focused on relatively high-need districts where at least 40 percent of students were eligible to receive free and reduced-price lunch.
resolved_title: Evaluation of the Teacher Potential Project (Mathematica, July 30, 2019)
notes: Districts recruited on a poverty threshold; within districts, schools were eligible if they had at least one novice ELA teacher and 45 minutes of ELA, then schools were randomized (70 schools, 18 districts, 12 states). All students of ELA teachers in study schools; no student rule. Kraft n 3932 to 9657 fits the one-year and two-year student samples. Long report; read Chapter II only.

evidence_quote: In order to be selected for Chicago TAP, a school had to have at least 75 percent of its students qualifying for free or reduced-price lunch.
resolved_title: An Evaluation of the Chicago Teacher Advancement Program (Chicago TAP) After Four Years: Final Report
notes: Chicago TAP was a pilot for high-need CPS schools; schools applied and had to meet the 75 percent FRL rule, then a lottery set the start year among applicant elementary schools (34 schools in the experimental sample). Selection on poverty at the school level; school-level application is not student opt-in. All K-8 students in study schools. Kraft n 7656 to 7661 matches the WWC grade 4 to 8 sample of 7,656.

evidence_quote: This study was conducted using data on 77 teachers at 11 Title I elementary schools in Aurora Public Schools for the 2013/14 and 2014/15 school years (see appendix A for more details). Participating schools had at least 80 percent of students eligible for the federal school lunch program, a proxy for low-income status.
resolved_title: Making an Impact: Impacts of the Retired Mentors for New Teachers program (REL 2017-225)
notes: The program pairs probationary teachers 'in high-need elementary schools' with retired mentors (theory of change, report p. 5), and every study school was Title I with at least 80 percent FRL against a district average of 70 percent, so the sites follow the program's own high-need rule; the report never says in one sentence that schools were chosen for poverty, hence medium confidence. Teachers randomized within schools; all students of those teachers in grades 1 to 5. Kraft n 964 to 1156 fits the Year 1 student samples by subject.

evidence_quote: The full study took place during 2015-2016 (implementation year) and 2016-2017 (impact year), involving 32 CPS schools, 96 fourth- and fifth-grade general and special education teachers, and approximately 1,500 fourth- and fifth- grade students
resolved_title: Assessing the impact of the Math for All professional development program on elementary school teachers and their students
notes: Codebook worked example. Thirty-two Chicago elementary schools randomized; schools average 92 percent free lunch but no poverty or performance criterion is stated. About half of grade 4 and 5 teachers per school agreed to take part and students needed parental consent for data, which are participation conditions, not program opt-in. Kraft n 392 (single math effect -0.05) is the first-year student analytic sample after attrition. WWC row counts 29 schools.

evidence_quote: For this study, 70 grade 8 Algebra I teachers were recruited from 15 school districts across California. Collectively, these districts are representative of the state in terms of geography, size, demographics, and socioeconomic status.
resolved_title: STEM Learning Opportunities Providing Equity: An Investing in Innovation (i3) Grant Final Evaluation Report (WestEd, Gallagher, Huang, and Van Matre, 2015)
notes: Teacher-level randomization; students placed in classrooms by routine district policy, no student rule. Districts had prior relationships with the grantee, not a need criterion. A confirmatory subquestion covers students below proficient on the grade 7 test, but Kraft's single effect (-0.08, n 2225) is consistent with the full grade 8 Algebra I sample, so mixed_samples = 0. DATA PROBLEM: the WWC match for study 340 is 82553, the SRI College-Ready Writers Program review by H. A. Gallagher, Woodworth, and Arshan, which belongs to study 341; the WWC sample text for 340 was therefore not used.

evidence_quote: The cut-off scores for student eligibility were set by Newark Public Schools (NPS), based on one standard deviation from the norm.
resolved_title: Striving Readers Study: Targeted and Whole-School Interventions, Year 5 (Westat, 2011)
notes: Newark Striving Readers. School rule: Title I eligible middle schools designated in need of improvement under NCLB, not already using READ 180 (report p. 5); 19 schools randomized. Student rule for the targeted READ 180 evaluation: NJASK reading subtest score below a district cut-off about one SD below the norm, that is, reading well below grade level. Kraft's 29 effects with n 436 to 2555 appear to mix the targeted sample (hundreds per grade or year) and the whole-school sample (all students in study schools), so mixed_samples = 1; both samples are targeted_low (student rule for targeted, INOI school rule for whole-school). Manual WWC match accepted 81694. Long report; read the executive summary and section 3.A only.

evidence_quote: A total of 68 schools were eligible, agreed to participate in the study, and met the study's requirement to identify their AR students before the schools were randomly assigned to condition.
resolved_title: Access to Algebra I: The Effects of Online Mathematics for Grade 8 Students (NCEE 2012-4021)
notes: Schools in Maine and Vermont were eligible if they served grade 8 and did not offer a stand-alone Algebra I course (school rule, not need-based); within them, schools identified algebra-ready (AR) students, 445 in all, as the analytic sample (student rule selecting advanced students, which the codebook puts under targeted_other). Kraft n 440 with one effect of 0.40 matches the AR algebra outcome. Mostly small rural schools, 94 percent Title I, but poverty was not a criterion.

evidence_quote: At each site, teachers, principals, and reading specialists identify students who are reading below grade level and consider the different reading interventions that are available to students.
resolved_title: Mobilizing Volunteer Tutors to Improve Student Literacy: Implementation, Impacts, and Costs of the Reading Partners Program (MDRC, March 2015)
notes: Students in grades 2 to 5 were referred to Reading Partners by school staff for reading below grade level, then randomized within school (1,265 students, 19 schools); all had parental consent for the pull-out tutoring study, so opt_in = 1 per the codebook. Schools were established Reading Partners sites in under-resourced, mostly schoolwide Title I schools with more capacity demand than seats, so level = both. Kraft n 492 to 1147 matches the WWC all-student and grade-band samples.
